claim: Neuronal oscillations putatively track speech in order to optimize sensory processing.
source: Neuronal oscillations putatively track speech in order to optimize sensory processing.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established theory in the field.

claim: It is unclear how isochronous brain oscillations can track pseudo-rhythmic speech input.
source: However, it is unclear how isochronous brain oscillations can track pseudo-rhythmic speech input.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current understanding.

claim: Speech time is dependent on content-based predictions flowing from internal language models.
source: Here we propose that oscillations can track pseudo-rhythmic speech when considering that speech time is dependent on content-based predictions flowing from internal language models.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Temporal dynamics of speech are dependent on the predictability of words in a sentence.
source: We show that temporal dynamics of speech are dependent on the predictability of words in a sentence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the corpus analysis presented in the Results section showing relationships between word predictability and timing.

claim: A computational model including oscillations, feedback, and inhibition is able to track pseudo-rhythmic speech input.
source: A computational model including oscillations, feedback, and inhibition is able to track pseudo-rhythmic speech input.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the STiMCON model simulations presented in the Results section.

claim: The model generates temporal phase codes as it processes, which are a candidate mechanism for carrying information forward in time.
source: As the model processes, it generates temporal phase codes, which are a candidate mechanism for carrying information forward in time.
evidence: This is shown through model simulations demonstrating phase-dependent activation patterns.

claim: The model is optimally sensitive to the natural temporal speech dynamics.
source: The model is optimally sensitive to the natural temporal speech dynamics and can explain empirical data on temporal speech illusions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the model validation showing optimal fit at specific oscillatory parameters (Figure 7).

claim: The model can explain empirical data on temporal speech illusions.
source: The model is optimally sensitive to the natural temporal speech dynamics and can explain empirical data on temporal speech illusions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through fitting the model to behavioral data from Ten Oever and Sack, 2015 (Figure 8).

claim: The temporal relationship between subsequent speech units allows for the online tracking of speech in order to optimize processing at relevant moments in time.
source: The temporal relationship between subsequent speech units allows for the online tracking of speech in order to optimize processing at relevant moments in time (Jones and Boltz, 1989; Large and Jones, 1999; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Ghitza and Greenberg, 2009; Ding et al., 2017; Arvaniti, 2009; Poeppel, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neural oscillations are a putative index of speech tracking.
source: Neural oscillations are a putative index of such tracking (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The range of onset time difference between speech units seems more variable than fixed oscillations can account for.
source: However, the range of onset time difference between speech units seems more variable than fixed oscillations can account for (Rimmele et al., 2018; Nolan and Jeon, 2014; Jadoul et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Word frequency significantly influences word duration.
source: Both number of syllables (coefficient = 0.1008, t(2843) = 75.47, p<0.001) as well as word frequency (coefficient = −0.022, t(2843) = −13.94, p<0.001) significantly influence the duration of the word.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis on the CGN corpus data.

claim: Number of syllables significantly influences word duration.
source: Both number of syllables (coefficient = 0.1008, t(2843) = 75.47, p<0.001) as well as word frequency (coefficient = −0.022, t(2843) = −13.94, p<0.001) significantly influence the duration of the word.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis on the CGN corpus data.

claim: Words with a low frequency can last three times as long as high-frequency words even within mono-syllabic words.
source: The effect is so strong that words with a low frequency can last three times as long as high-frequency words (even within mono-syllabic words).
evidence: This is an observation from the corpus analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: The syllabic rate varies between 3 and 8 Hz.
source: We found that the syllabic rate varies between 3 and 8 Hz as previously reported (Figure 2E, right; Ding et al., 2017; Pellegrino and Coupé, 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The more syllables there are in a word, the higher the syllabic rate.
source: However, the more syllables there are in a word, the higher this rate (ρ = 0.676, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the corpus data.

claim: RNN prediction is a significant predictor of word onset differences.
source: All predictors except word frequency of the previous word showed a significant effect (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the regression analysis presented in Table 1, where RNN prediction has t(4837) = −7.163, p<0.001.

claim: The RNN predictor captures more variance than the bigram model in predicting word onset differences.
source: The RNN predictor could capture more variance than the bigram model, suggesting that word duration is modulated by the level of predictability within a fuller context than just the conditional probability of the current word given the previous word (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the regression analysis comparing RNN and bigram predictors.

claim: Words are systematically lengthened when the next word is not strongly predicted by the internal model.
source: These results suggest that words are systematically lengthened (or pauses are added. However, the same predictors are also significant when excluding sentences containing pauses) when the next word is not strongly predicted by the internal model.
evidence: This is inferred from the regression analysis showing negative relationship between RNN prediction and onset differences.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between variance of RNN predictions within a sentence and theta power.
source: We found a weak, but significant negative correlation (r = −0.062, p<0.001; Figure 3D) in line with our hypothesis.
evidence: This is shown through correlation analysis of prediction variance and FFT power.

claim: The more variable the predictions within a sentence, the lower the peak power value.
source: This suggests that the more variable the predictions within a sentence, the lower the peak power value is.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation between prediction variance and theta power.

claim: The timing at which different nodes reach activation depends on the level of feedback provided in the STiMCON model.
source: When we present this model with different sensory inputs at an isochronous rhythm of 4 Hz, it is evident that the timing at which different nodes reach activation depends on the level of feedback that is provided (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Within the STiMCON model, the activation of nodes is robust to some timing variation in the environment.
source: This means that within this model (and any oscillating model) the activation of nodes is robust to some timing variation in the environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing that timing variation in input results in smaller variation in activation timing (1:6.9 ratio).

claim: A stimulus timing that varies between 130 ms only reaches the first supra-threshold response with 19 ms variation in the model.
source: A stimulus timing that varies between 130 ms (e.g., from −59 to +72 in the /cake/ line; excluding the non-linear section of the line) only reaches the first supra-threshold response with 19 ms variation in the model (translating to a reduction of 53–8% of the cycle of the ongoing oscillation, i.e., a 1:6.9 ratio).
evidence: This is calculated from the model simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The model with no content predictions has overall lowest power but has the strongest 4 Hz response around isochronous presentation at high stimulus intensities.
source: The first thing that is evident is that the model with no content predictions has overall lowest power, but has the strongest 4 Hz response around isochronous presentation (odd word offset of 0 ms) at high stimulus intensities (Figure 6B–D) following closely the acoustic input.
evidence: This is shown through FFT analysis of model outputs in Figure 6.

claim: For the low to high predictability condition, 4 Hz power is strongest when the predictable odd stimulus is shifted to an earlier time point.
source: For the low to high predictability condition, the curve seems to be shifted to the left such that 4 Hz power is strongest when the predictable odd stimulus is shifted to an earlier time point (low–high condition).
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations presented in Figure 6.

claim: Even though stimulus input is non-isochronous, the interaction with the internal model can still create a potential isochronous structure in the brain.
source: These results show that even though stimulus input is non-isochronous, the interaction with the internal model can still create a potential isochronous structure in the brain (see Meyer et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the model simulations showing stronger rhythmic responses to matched pseudo-rhythmic input.

claim: STiMCON's expected word-to-word onset differences can be fitted to the word-to-word onset differences found in the CGN corpus.
source: Results show a modulation of the R2 dependent on the amplitude and phase offset of the oscillation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through regression analysis fitting model predictions to corpus data.

claim: The optimal transformation of RNN predictions through the oscillatory model automatically alters a highly skewed prediction distribution toward a more normal distribution of relative time shifts.
source: Interestingly, the optimal transformation seemed to automatically alter a highly skewed prediction distribution (Figure 7B) toward a more normal distribution of relative time shifts (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown through comparison of distributions in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: STiMCON can show a phase-dependent effect on which node is activated first for ambiguous stimuli.
source: Results showed that for some ambiguous stimuli, the delay determines which node is activated first, modulating the ultimate percept of the participant (Figure 8A, also see Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations of ambiguous /da/-/ga/ stimuli.

claim: The STiMCON model can fit behavioral data from Ten Oever and Sack, 2015 at an average explained variance of 43% for first node activation analysis.
source: For the first node activation analysis, we found that our model could fit the data at an average explained variance of 43% (30% and 58% for 6.25 Hz and 10 Hz, respectively; Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is shown through grid search fitting of model parameters to empirical data.

claim: For the average activity analysis, the STiMCON model achieved a fit with 83% explained variance.
source: For the average activity analysis, we found a fit with 83% explained variance.
evidence: This is shown through grid search fitting of model parameters to empirical data.

claim: STiMCON does better than a fixed-frequency sinus fit in explaining temporal speech illusions.
source: Thus, STiMCON does better than a fixed-frequency sinus fit.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of Akaike information criterion values between the model and sinus fits.

claim: All three key features of the model (inhibition, feedback, and oscillations) are required to fit the empirical data on temporal speech illusions.
source: Results showed for both outcome measures that the full model showed the best performance. Without the oscillation, the models could not even fit better than the mean of the model (R2 < 0).
evidence: This is shown through ablation analysis removing each component and comparing model performance.

claim: Mean word duration in the CGN corpus was 0.392 s with an average standard deviation of 0.094 s.
source: Mean word duration was 0.392 s, with an average standard deviation of 0.094 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the corpus analysis.

claim: The reported speech rates fall within the generally reported ranges for syllables (5.2 Hz) and words (3.7 Hz).
source: The reported rates fall within the generally reported ranges for syllables (5.2 Hz) and words (3.7 Hz; Ding et al., 2017; Pellegrino and Coupé, 2011).
evidence: This compares the corpus analysis results to prior literature.

claim: Adding an interaction term between word frequency and number of syllables did not significantly improve the regression model.
source: Adding an interaction term did not significantly improve the model (F (1,2843) = 1.320, p=0.251; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown through statistical testing of the regression model.

claim: There is a strong correlation between word length and mean word duration for number of characters (ρ = 0.824, p<0.001).
source: Obviously, there is a strong correlation between word length and mean word duration (number of characters 0.824, p<0.001; number of syllables: ρ = 0.808, p<0.001; for number of syllables already shown above; Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is shown through correlation analysis of the corpus data.

claim: There is a strong correlation between word length and mean word duration for number of syllables (ρ = 0.808, p<0.001).
source: Obviously, there is a strong correlation between word length and mean word duration (number of characters 0.824, p<0.001; number of syllables: ρ = 0.808, p<0.001; for number of syllables already shown above; Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is shown through correlation analysis of the corpus data.

claim: The correlation between word length and standard deviation of word duration is much lower than for mean duration (number of characters: ρ = 0.269, p<0.001; number of syllables: ρ = 0.292, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, this correlation is present, but much lower for the standard deviation of word duration (number of characters: ρ = 0.269, p<0.001; number of syllables: ρ = 0.292, p<0.001).
evidence: This is shown through correlation analysis of the corpus data.

claim: The increase in character rate with word length was less strong (ρ = 0.499, p<0.001) than for syllabic rate.
source: This increase was less strong for the character rate (ρ = 0.499, p<0.001; Figure 2D, right).
evidence: This is shown through correlation analysis of the corpus data.

claim: The syllabic/character rate depends on the number of characters/syllables within a word and is not an independent temporal unit.
source: These results show that the syllabic/character rate depends on the number of characters /syllables within a word and is not an independent temporal unit (Ghitza, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analyses showing rate increases with word length.

claim: Using the trained RNN model as a predictor was necessary; entering RNN predictions after the first training cycle did not result in a significant predictor.
source: Importantly, it was necessary to use the trained RNN model as a predictor; entering the RNN predictions after the first training cycle (of a total of 100) did not results in a significant predictor (t(4837) = −1.191, p=0.234).
evidence: This is shown through regression analysis comparing trained vs. untrained RNN predictions.

claim: Adding word frequency of the current word did not add significant information to the regression model.
source: Also adding the predictor word frequency of the current word did not add significant information to the model (F(1, 4830) = 0.2048, p=0.651).
evidence: This is shown through statistical testing of the regression model.

claim: RNN predictions have no effect on the duration of the word that has to be uttered.
source: We also investigate whether RNN predictions have an influence on the duration of the word that has to be uttered. We found no effect on the duration (Supporting Table 1).
evidence: This is shown through regression analysis testing the effect of RNN predictions on word duration.

claim: When repeating the sentence isochrony analysis on the envelope, no significant effect was found.
source: When we repeated the analysis on the envelope, we did not find a significant effect.
evidence: This is a null result from the analysis of prediction variance and envelope power.

claim: The CGN corpus consists of elaborated annotations of over 900 hr of spoken Dutch and Flemish words.
source: This corpus consists of elaborated annotations of over 900 hr of spoken Dutch and Flemish words.
evidence: This is a description of the data source used in the study.

claim: The cleaned CGN dataset resulted in 574,726 annotated words with 3096 unique words.
source: This resulted in 574,726 annotated words with 3096 unique words.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the processed corpus data.

claim: 2,048 of the words were recognized in the Dutch Wordforms database in CELEX.
source: Two thousand and forty-eight of the words were recognized in the Dutch Wordforms database in CELEX (Version 3.1) in order to extract the word frequency as well as the number of syllables per word (later needed to fit a regression model).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the data processing.

claim: The final RNN model includes an LSTM with 300 units.
source: The final model we use here includes a LSTM with 300 units.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the RNN model used.

claim: The RNN model consisted of an embedding layer, a recurrent layer with a tanh activation function, and a dense output layer with a softmax activation.
source: The model consisted of an embedding layer (pretrained; github.com/coosto/dutch-word-embeddings), a recurrent layer with a tanh activation function, and a dense output layer with a softmax activation.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the RNN model.

claim: Pseudo-rhythmicity is fully natural to the brain when speech timing depends on internal language models.
source: Thus, the phase of arrival depends on the internal model of the producer and the expected phase of arrival depends on the internal model of the receiver (Figure 1D). If this is true, pseudo-rhythmicity is fully natural to the brain, and it provides a means to use time or arrival phase as a content indicator.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the proposed model.

claim: Current oscillatory models of speech parsing do not integrate the constraints flowing from an internal linguistic model into the temporal structure of the brain response.
source: Current oscillatory models of speech parsing do not integrate the constraints flowing from an internal linguistic model into the temporal structure of the brain response.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models in the literature.

claim: The primary auditory cortex is likely still mostly modulated by the acoustic pseudo-rhythmic input and only later brain areas follow more closely the constraints posed by the language model of the brain.
source: For example, it is likely that the primary auditory cortex is still mostly modulated by the acoustic pseudo-rhythmic input and only later brain areas follow more closely the constraints posed by the language model of the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural implementation of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Predictive mechanisms likely operate on syllabic levels as well as higher linguistic levels.
source: It is likely that predictive mechanisms also operate on these higher linguistic levels as well as on syllabic levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Syllables are shortened when the following syllabic content is known versus producing syllables in isolation.
source: It is known, for example, that syllables are shortened when the following syllabic content is known versus producing syllables in isolation (Pluymaekers et al., 2005a; Lehiste, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: Syllables part of more frequent words are generally shortened.
source: Interactions also occur as syllables part of more frequent words are generally shortened (Pluymaekers et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior empirical work.

claim: When the internal model and the onset timings do not match, internal model phase and/or frequency shifts are still required.
source: However, when the internal model and the onset timings do not match, the internal model phase and/or frequency shift are still required and need to be incorporated (see e.g. Rimmele et al., 2018; Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020).
evidence: This is a limitation of the current model and suggestion for future work.

claim: Phase resetting models typically deal with pseudo-rhythmicity by shifting the phase of ongoing oscillations in response to a word that is offset to the mean frequency of the input.
source: Phase resetting models typically deal with pseudo-rhythmicity by shifting the phase of ongoing oscillations in response to a word that is offset to the mean frequency of the input (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Doelling et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes alternative models in the literature.

claim: Phase resetting models cannot explain how the brain uses what/when dependencies in the environment to infer the content of the word.
source: We believe that this cannot explain how the brain uses what/when dependencies in the environment to infer the content of the word (e.g., later words are likely a less predictable word).
evidence: This is a critique of alternative models based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The best way forward is likely to extend coupling between brain oscillations and speech acoustics with the coupling of brain oscillations to brain activity patterns of internal models.
source: Therefore, the best way forward is likely to extend coupling between brain oscillations and speech acoustics (Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020), with the coupling of brain oscillations to brain activity patterns of internal models (Cumin and Unsworth, 2007).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future theoretical development.

claim: It is unlikely that the RNN captures the wide complexities of the language model in the brain.
source: However, it is unlikely that the RNN captures the wide complexities of the language model in the brain.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the RNN as a proxy for internal language models.

claim: Utilizing the RNN as a proxy for internal language model makes a tacit assumption that language is fundamentally statistical or associative in nature.
source: Utilizing the RNN as a proxy for our internal language model makes a tacit assumption that language is fundamentally statistical or associative in nature, and does not posit the derivation or generation of knowledge of grammar from the input (Chater, 2001; McClelland and Elman, 1986).
evidence: This is a theoretical discussion of the assumptions underlying the modeling approach.

claim: A natural feature of the STiMCON model is that time can act as a cue for content implemented as a phase code.
source: A natural feature of our model is that time can act as a cue for content implemented as a phase code (Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a property of the model demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The phase code in the STiMCON model unravels as an ordered list of predictability strength of the internal model.
source: This code unravels as an ordered list of predictability strength of the internal model.
evidence: This is a property of the model demonstrated through simulations.

claim: If speech nodes have a different base activity, ambiguous stimulus interpretation should depend on the time/phase of presentation.
source: We predict that if speech nodes have a different base activity, ambiguous stimulus interpretation should dependent on the time/phase of presentation (see Ten Oever and Sack, 2015; Ten Oever et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is supported by cited empirical work.

claim: When modifying the time of presentation with a neutral entrainer, no obvious phase effect was reported.
source: For the speech rate effect, when modifying the time of presentation with a neutral entrainer (summed sinusoidals with random phase), no obvious phase effect was reported (Bosker and Kösem, 2017).
evidence: This is a null result from prior empirical work.

claim: The temporal dynamics of speech signals needs to be integrated with the temporal dynamics of brain signals.
source: The temporal dynamics of speech signals needs to be integrated with the temporal dynamics of brain signals.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the approach taken in the paper.

claim: It is unnecessary and unlikely that the exact duration of speech matches with the exact duration of brain processes.
source: However, it is unnecessary (and unlikely) that the exact duration of speech matches with the exact duration of brain processes.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on knowledge of temporal processing in the brain.

claim: Temporal expansion or squeezing of stimulus inputs occur regularly in the brain.
source: Temporal expansion or squeezing of stimulus inputs occur regularly in the brain (Eagleman et al., 2005; Pariyadath and Eagleman, 2007), and this temporal morphing also maps to duration (Eagleman, 2008; Terao et al., 2008; Ulrich et al., 2006) or order illusions (Vroomen and Keetels, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work on temporal perception.

claim: The STiMCON model predicts increased rhythmic responses for non-isochronous speech matching the internal model.
source: Our model predicts increased rhythmic responses for non-isochronous speech matching the internal model.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The perceived rhythmicity of speech could be an illusion generated by a rhythmic brain signal.
source: The perceived rhythmicity of speech could therefore also be an illusion generated by a rhythmic brain signal somewhere in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results.

claim: Speech is more isochronous during production of lists.
source: Two examples are the production of lists (Jefferson, 1990) and infant-directed speech (Fernald, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior empirical work.

claim: Speech is more isochronous during infant-directed speech.
source: Two examples are the production of lists (Jefferson, 1990) and infant-directed speech (Fernald, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior empirical work.

claim: Speech is more isochronous during poems, during emotional conversation, and in noisy situations.
source: Other examples in which speech is more isochronous is during poems, during emotional conversation (Hawkins, 2014), and in noisy situations (Bosker and Cooke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: A producer might proactively adapt its speech rhythm to the expectations of the internal model of the receiver to align better with the predictions from the receiver's model.
source: The infant-directed speech also illustrates that a producer might proactively adapt its speech rhythm to the expectations of the internal model of the receiver to align better with the predictions from the receiver's model (Figure 9B; similar to when you are speaking to somebody that is just learning a new language).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the theoretical framework and examples from infant-directed speech.

claim: When there is a flat constraint distribution over an utterance, the acoustics of speech should naturally be more isochronous.
source: When there is a flat constraint distribution over an utterance (e.g., when probabilities are uniform over the utterance), the acoustics of speech should naturally be more isochronous (Figures 9A and 3D,E).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model supported by the simulation results.

claim: If speech timing matches the internal language model, brain responses should be more isochronous even if the acoustics are not.
source: If speech timing matches the internal language model, brain responses should be more isochronous even if the acoustics are not (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model supported by the simulation results.

claim: The more similar the internal language models of two speakers, the more effective they are in 'entraining' each other's brain.
source: The more similar the internal language models of two speakers, the more effective they are in 'entraining' each other's brain.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical framework.

claim: If speakers suspect their listener to have a flatter constraint distribution than themselves, they adjust to the distribution by speaking more isochronous.
source: If speakers suspect their listener to have a flatter constraint distribution than themselves (e.g., the environment is noisy, or the speakers are in a second language context), they adjust to the distribution by speaking more isochronous (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical framework.

claim: One adjusts the weight of the constraint distribution to a hierarchical level when needed, such as adjusting to the rhythm of primary auditory cortex instead of higher order language models when there is noise.
source: One adjusts the weight of the constraint distribution to a hierarchical level when needed. For example, when there is noise, participants adjust to the rhythm of primary auditory cortex instead of higher order language models. As a consequence, they speak more isochronous.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the proposed mechanism might operate in different contexts.

claim: Pseudo-rhythmicity in speech is in part a consequence of top-down predictions flowing from an internal model of language.
source: We argued that pseudo-rhythmicity in speech is in part a consequence of top-down predictions flowing from an internal model of language.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper supported by corpus analysis and modeling.

claim: Pseudo-rhythmicity is created by a speaker and expected by a receiver if they have overlapping internal language models.
source: This pseudo-rhythmicity is created by a speaker and expected by a receiver if they have overlapping internal language models.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical framework and modeling results.

claim: Oscillatory tracking of pseudo-rhythmic speech does not need to be hampered by the pseudo-rhythmicity, but can use temporal variations as a cue to extract content information.
source: Oscillatory tracking of this signal does not need to be hampered by the pseudo-rhythmicity, but can use temporal variations as a cue to extract content information since the phase of activation parametrically relates to the likelihood of an input relative to the internal model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Brain responses can be more isochronous to pseudo-rhythmic compared to isochronous speech if they follow the temporal delays imposed by the internal model.
source: Brain responses can even be more isochronous to pseudo-rhythmic compared to isochronous speech if they follow the temporal delays imposed by the internal model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results shown in Figure 6.
